title: Handling a difficult person on the crew
moduleTitle: Shared: Growing and managing a team
audience: Team leaders who have a crew member whose behaviour is making the work harder for others.
learningOutcomes: Recognise four common patterns of difficult behaviour and the effect each has on a crew.
Apply a private, specific conversation approach that describes impact without attacking the person.
Decide when to follow up and when to escalate to the supervisor.

instruction.heading: Check yourself first
instruction.body: Before raising anything, test whether the behaviour is the true issue or whether your own reaction is amplifying it. Notice whether you have had the same kind of difficulty with other people. Talk it through with a trusted colleague so you can see the situation clearly. Strong feelings such as anger, embarrassment or fear are normal, but they should not set the course of the conversation.

instruction.heading: Four patterns and what they do
instruction.body: Some workers are constantly critical and rarely satisfied. Some present themselves as the expert and talk down to others. Some go quiet, agree in the meeting and then do little. Some are forceful and insist on their own way. Each pattern affects the crew differently. The critic drains morale, the self-promoter undermines colleagues, the quiet worker shifts the load, and the forceful worker can intimidate others into silence. Identify the pattern, because it shapes the conversation.

instruction.heading: Speak privately and follow up
instruction.body: Trying to change someone's character in a group rarely works and often makes the person defend the behaviour more. Instead, understand what the person values, because that often explains their choices. Speak to them in private, describe the specific behaviour and its effect on the job, and agree a small number of specific steps. Follow up after a set time. If the behaviour continues or escalates, write down the facts and take them to the supervisor. Where the behaviour is hurtful or intimidating, limit contact and keep the working relationship to what the job needs.

procedure: Write down the specific behaviour, the date, who was present and its effect on the job.
Check whether you have had similar difficulty before and whether the cause is in your own reaction.
Arrange a private conversation and describe the behaviour and its effect using 'I' statements.
Ask what the person needs or values, then agree one or two specific actions.
Set a date to check progress and record the outcome.
If the behaviour continues or is hurtful, refer it to the supervisor with your written notes.

workedExamples.situation: A crew member repeatedly tells newer workers that their methods are wrong, in front of clients, and the newer workers have started avoiding the crew van.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the lead do first, and when should the supervisor be involved?
workedExamples.reasoning: The lead records the incidents, speaks to the worker privately about how the comments affect the team's work, asks what standard the worker is protecting, and agrees one action such as raising method questions at briefings. If the comments continue, the lead refers the written notes to the supervisor.

equipmentAndPpe: Notebook for dated notes. Standard PPE on site.

commonErrors.error: Trying to change the person's character in front of the crew.
commonErrors.prevention: Speak privately and describe the behaviour, not the character.

commonErrors.error: Letting the situation run for months and then reacting strongly.
commonErrors.prevention: Address the behaviour early while the facts are clear.

commonErrors.error: Joining in the gossip about the difficult worker.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep discussions factual and limited to the people who need to know.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Bullying, harassment and discrimination are handled through the business's procedure and may have legal implications.

qualityStandard: The notes name the behaviour, the date, the people present and the effect on the job.
The conversation agrees at least one specific action and a later check-in date.
documentationEvidence: Follow-up record and, where used, the referral to the supervisor.
summary: Check yourself before acting on a difficult behaviour.
Identify the pattern, then speak privately about the specific behaviour and its effect.
Follow up on a date, and refer continuing or hurtful behaviour with written notes.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best first step before addressing a difficult crew member?
options: Confront the worker in front of the crew and call them out for the mistake
Check whether your own reaction is shaping the problem and record the facts
Ask the client to deal with it and tell them the crew is at fault
Move the worker to another crew immediately and do not tell them why

knowledgeChecks.question: Which opening describes the behaviour and its effect without attacking the person?
options: You are negative, and nobody on the crew wants to work with you and you always complain about the job
You need a better attitude and you should sort it out this week or be moved to another crew
When you comment on other people's methods in front of clients, the newer workers start avoiding the crew
Everyone thinks you are difficult and the team leader is fed up with you and the client has said so

knowledgeChecks.question: When should a lead refer a difficult behaviour to the supervisor?
options: Straight away, without any private talk, to keep it fair and to show the crew it is treated the same
Only after the worker has resigned and the crew and the client have been told about it
Only when a client complains publicly and the crew has seen it happen twice this month
When the behaviour continues after a private conversation or is hurtful, with written notes
